questions.text: Listen to these two words: 'bit' and 'bite.' Which one has a long I sound, like in the word 'kite'?
questions.explanation: 'Bite' has the long I sound. The silent E at the end makes the vowel say its name.

questions.text: Listen to these sounds: /sh/ /i/ /p/. Blend them together. What word do they make?
questions.explanation: Blending /sh/, /i/, and /p/ together makes the word 'ship.'

questions.text: What is the middle vowel sound in the word 'hop'?
questions.explanation: The middle vowel sound in 'hop' is /o/, a short O sound.

questions.text: How many separate sounds do you hear in the word 'flag'? Say each sound: /f/ /l/ /a/ /g/.
Which word begins with the 'sh' sound, like in 'shell'?
questions.explanation: 'Shark' begins with the digraph 'sh,' which makes the /sh/ sound heard at the start of 'shell.'

questions.text: Which word has two syllables? Clap as you say each one.
questions.explanation: 'Basket' has two syllables: 'bas' and 'ket.' The other words each have only one syllable.

questions.passage: Omar found a tiny green frog by the pond. He watched it jump three times before it disappeared into the tall grass.
questions.text: Where did Omar find the frog?
questions.explanation: The story says Omar found the frog by the pond.

questions.passage: A little turtle walked very slowly to the river. She stopped to rest many times. When she finally got there, she jumped in and swam fast and free.
questions.text: What is the main message of this story?
options: Turtles do not like to walk.
Slow and steady effort can get you to your goal.
Rivers are the best place to swim.
You should always stop and rest.
questions.explanation: Even though the turtle walked slowly and stopped to rest, she kept going and finally reached the river, showing that steady effort pays off.

questions.passage: Lily wanted to build a sandcastle, but the sand was too dry. She got a bucket of water and wet the sand. Then her castle stood tall and strong.
questions.text: What problem did Lily have, and how did she solve it?
options: She had no bucket; she borrowed one.
The sand was too dry; she added water.
The castle fell down; she built it again.
She was too tired; she took a rest.
questions.explanation: Lily's problem was that the sand was too dry. She solved it by getting a bucket of water to wet the sand.

questions.passage: The warm sun kissed her cheeks. A sweet breeze danced through the flowers.
questions.text: The phrase 'the warm sun kissed her cheeks' helps you imagine how something feels. What sense does it appeal to?
questions.explanation: The phrase describes warmth on her cheeks, which is a feeling you sense with your skin — the sense of touch.

questions.passage: Bees live together in a hive. They work as a team to make honey from flower nectar.
questions.text: What do bees make from flower nectar?
questions.explanation: The text says bees make honey from flower nectar.

questions.passage: Penguins huddle together when it is very cold. Huddling means pressing close to stay warm.
questions.text: Based on the passage, what does the word 'huddle' mean?
options: To eat a lot of food
questions.explanation: The passage explains that huddling means pressing close together to stay warm.

questions.text: Which sentence uses a proper noun correctly?
questions.explanation: The name of a specific dog, Spot, is a proper noun and must begin with a capital letter.

questions.text: Which sentence uses the correct verb form to match the subject?
options: The birds are flying south yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'The birds fly south' is correct because plural subjects like 'birds' use the base form of the verb without an -s ending.
The sentence should start with a capital M, and the month July is a proper noun that must be capitalized.
